analysis.one_liner: Makes companies prove they can pay to clean up toxic sites before taxpayers get stuck with the bill.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have forced the EPA to finally enforce a 1980 mandate requiring polluters to prove they can pay for toxic cleanups, never advanced past its Senate committee referral and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the EPA to finish writing rules, first required by Congress in 1980, that force companies handling hazardous substances to prove up front they can pay for potential cleanups, rather than leaving taxpayers to pick up the tab when a company goes bankrupt. It would have required companies to notify the EPA when they file for bankruptcy, disclose their corporate relationships so liabilities cannot be shifted around, and let bankruptcy trustees claw back assets moved to dodge cleanup debts up to 10 years earlier. It died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently bear cleanup costs when polluting companies go bankrupt or shield assets in corporate affiliates. The bill's own findings cite a 1,244-site Superfund backlog and an average taxpayer cleanup cost of $12 million per site, and note the industry tax that once funded cleanups has lapsed. Residents near contaminated sites would also benefit from faster remediation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have required the EPA, within 18 months, to finalize the financial assurance regulations under CERCLA section 108(b) that Congress first mandated in 1980 and that the EPA had never issued, so companies handling hazardous substances would have to prove ability to pay before a cleanup is needed rather than after.

Owners and operators of covered facilities that file for bankruptcy would have had to notify the EPA, estimate the environmental impacts and cleanup costs of their activities, and disclose all current and former corporate relationships such as parents, subsidiaries, and affiliates, closing off the corporate-structure maneuvers the bill's findings say are used to shirk liabilities.

The bill would have extended the bankruptcy trustee's power to unwind fraudulent transfers from 1 year to 10 years before a bankruptcy filing, when the debtor had environmental cleanup liabilities and moved assets with intent to hinder, delay, or defraud creditors on those liabilities.

It would have directed the EPA to make full use of administrative offsets and liens on assets when enforcing cleanup obligations, and to prioritize rules for industries with a record of defaulting on environmental liabilities.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that produce, transport, treat, store, or dispose of hazardous substances — chemical manufacturers, hardrock mining operations, refineries, and waste treatment and disposal facilities — would bear the cost of securing and maintaining financial assurance for potential cleanup liabilities, and would face longer exposure to having asset transfers undone in bankruptcy. Some of these compliance costs could ultimately be passed to consumers in prices.

drawbacks.text: The financial assurance requirements would impose real upfront compliance costs on hazardous-substance handlers — bonds, insurance, or proof of net worth — and some of those costs would likely be passed through to consumers in the prices of chemicals, fuels, and minerals.

The 10-year lookback for unwinding transfers in bankruptcy goes far beyond the standard 1- and 2-year windows in bankruptcy law; even limited to transfers made with intent to defraud, it creates a long period of uncertainty for companies with any environmental exposure and their lenders and counterparties.

The bill was a single-chamber directive with no Republican cosponsors and no Senate debate, so the costs and feasibility of the deadlines — including an annual rulemaking cycle for additional facility classes — were never tested in committee or on the floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — making polluters prove they can pay for cleanups instead of leaving them to taxpayers when companies fold — addresses a documented gap: the EPA had ignored a 1980 statutory mandate for over 25 years, the Superfund industry tax had lapsed, and the bill cites a 1,244-site cleanup backlog averaging $12 million per site. The compliance costs are real and would be felt in prices, and the 10-year bankruptcy lookback is aggressive even with its fraud-intent limit, but the bill only compels the EPA to implement authority it already had. On balance the public benefit outweighs the cost, and the bill's failure means the status quo — taxpayers absorbing defaulted cleanup costs — continued.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on June 14, 2006, with Sens. Barbara Boxer and Jim Jeffords, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action was ever recorded: the committee held no markup, the Senate never debated it, and there was no vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

The bill's findings stated that the EPA had failed for more than 25 years to implement the financial assurance mandate Congress enacted in 1980, and cited a Government Accountability Office report finding that agencies could not even track how many of the more than 231,000 businesses that filed for bankruptcy between 1998 and 2003 carried environmental liabilities.

The bill's findings noted that the corporate tax that once funded Superfund cleanups had lapsed, leaving taxpayers to cover a growing backlog of 1,244 National Priorities List sites averaging $12 million each to clean up.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies with hazardous-substance liabilities — chemical, mining, refining, and waste-disposal operators — were better off, because they continued to face no federal requirement to prove they could pay for cleanups and could still limit liabilities through bankruptcy and corporate restructuring, leaving those costs with taxpayers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Polluting companies that avoided cleanup costs

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Chemical, hardrock mining, and waste-disposal industries
against.role: Facilities that would be subject to the financial assurance requirements
against.what_they_did: These industries have long opposed CERCLA financial assurance rules, which would require them to post bonds or prove net worth for potential cleanup liabilities.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three sponsors were two Democrats and one Independent with no Republican cosponsors, but because the committee never acted and no vote was ever taken, the record shows only the sponsor lineup, not how the chamber would have split.

industries.note: The bill would have required chemical producers handling hazardous substances to post financial assurance and prove net worth for potential cleanup costs, ending their ability to leave those costs to taxpayers through bankruptcy. Its interest in avoiding those requirements runs directly against taxpayers who otherwise pay for defaulted cleanups.

Mining operations are among the largest sources of unreimbursed Superfund cleanup costs, and the bill directed the EPA to prioritize rules for high-risk classes of facilities and industries with records of defaulting on environmental liabilities. Taxpayers near abandoned mines currently absorb those cleanup bills.

industries.industry: Waste treatment, storage, and disposal facilities
industries.note: Facilities with corrective action permits or orders under the Solid Waste Disposal Act would have had to enter financial assurance agreements covering all potential response costs, and notify the EPA of any bankruptcy filing with full corporate-relationship disclosures. Their cost of doing business rises, but so does the guarantee that cleanups get funded.

A financial assurance mandate creates a large new market for the environmental insurance and surety products companies would need to demonstrate ability to pay. This gain comes only as a cost to the regulated companies, not to the public.
